documents: Yang, Smith & Gupta (2023), Basin Research 35:214-243, published paper (PDF)

entry.evidence: Given a large number of possible variables and the difficulty of measuring interactions, this makes estimation of the importance of each variable challenging.

steps.action: The authors pose the question of the relative importance, through time, of the variables controlling palaeo-landscape evolution and basin fill in the Gippsland Basin.
steps.quote: The primary aim was to identify the relative importance of the controlling variables through time.

steps.action: They build a realistic 3D structural-stratigraphic model in Petrel from open-file 2D/3D seismic, more than 1250 wells and bores, gravity data and micropalaeontological water depths, to serve as the reference for the simulations.
steps.quote: the first step was to build a 3D realistic structural and stratigraphic model

steps.action: They define an uncertainty framework of 13 Badlands input variables with low, reference and high ranges (Table 1), based on expert knowledge, test runs, the realistic model and the literature.
steps.quote: A total of 13 variables or uncertainties were selected as the main variables used as input for the Badlands simulations

steps.action: They construct a Reference Case Badlands model with approximate mid values, constrained by the realistic model, and use it for sensitivity analysis of candidate variables and ranges.
steps.quote: A Reference Case model was constructed in Badlands using constraints from the realistic 3D geological model

steps.action: They take published field values of erodibility k and the exponents m and n from other basins (Table 2) as starting ranges for testing.
steps.quote: Typical values for these variables are known from many landscape studies

steps.action: They run first sensitivity simulations from an initial topography rescaled from the present day, with mountains only to the north and west.
steps.quote: The first sensitivity simulations were started using a topographic map with mountains in the north and west only

steps.action: They compare the underfilled, early open-marine result with well data and the known timing of marine onset (after 90 Ma) and find a mismatch.
steps.quote: This does not fit the onshore or offshore well data

steps.action: Through a series of sensitivity runs, they infer that the initial topography needed highlands to the north, south and east to balance the Early Cretaceous sediment budget.
steps.quote: only the models run with mountains to the north, south and east provide enough sediment input into the Gippsland Basin

steps.action: They compare the inferred highland configuration with published provenance and drill data (Edwards & Baker 1943; Jones & Veevers 1982) and find it consistent.
steps.quote: are consistent with studies of the sources for the clastic sediment in the basin

steps.action: They run the forward models with and without compaction to test the effect of rescaling the isopachs. With compaction, sediment supply was insufficient at some time steps.
steps.quote: The Badlands forward models were run with and without compaction to test the effect of re-scaling due to compaction

steps.action: They attribute the compaction-run sediment deficit to a larger catchment or higher highlands, keep compaction off for the main ED runs, and defer compaction to future work.
steps.quote: This is not thought to be critical here since the aim is to assess the relative importance of the landscape evolution factors

steps.action: They generate preliminary uplift (eroded-section) maps from published exhumation estimates (apatite fission track, vitrinite reflectance, river profiles), tested by sensitivity runs with thicker and thinner isopachs (Figure 6). They find median land elevation is about a quarter of the missing-section thickness.
steps.quote: Several sensitivity tests were run based on the published results to generate the preliminary uplift maps

steps.action: They run sensitivity tests for k, m and n of the stream power law to find ranges matching the realistic model, and calibrate the elevation-precipitation relation with the Australian monthly rainfall dataset.
steps.quote: sensitivity tests were run for k, m and n to find the range of possible values that matched the data in the realistic 3D model

steps.action: They screen the uncertainty framework down to 12 two-level variables plus three-level sea level with six interactions, and use GSAT to generate a 22-scenario fractional factorial design (Table 4).
steps.quote: The ED matrix generated by GSAT has 22 scenarios as given in Table 4

steps.action: They run the 22 designed scenarios in Badlands at 1 Myr steps from 137 Ma to the present, giving 3014 maps.
steps.quote: The 22 scenarios were run in Badlands using a set of python scripts at time steps of 1 million year increments.

steps.action: They import six key horizon maps per scenario into Petrel and compute node-by-node difference maps against the realistic model, summarised by mean, standard deviation and mean sum.
steps.quote: The Badlands response maps imported into Petrel were used to calculate a map of the difference or deviation in metres

steps.action: They import the difference-map responses into GSAT, fit multivariate response equations, and run ANOVA to estimate the significance of each factor and interaction.
steps.quote: to test the significance of each factor and all the interactions between factors

steps.action: Preliminary tornado charts showed erodibility and m dominating and masking other effects, so they adjust those ranges toward field data for the final runs.
steps.quote: The ranges were adjusted for these variables in the final simulation runs to better represent the field data

steps.action: They plot the mean sums against summed standard deviations for all scenarios (Figure 11). Most scenarios fit; 6 and 4 fit poorly and 7, 13 and 18 very poorly.
steps.quote: most scenarios are reasonable fits to the data and highlights the cases with poor fits (scenarios 6 and 4)

steps.action: They estimate response equations and variable significance separately for each stratigraphic interval (Table 5).
steps.quote: The results allow assessment of the fit to the scenarios and estimate the significance of each variable for the different time periods

steps.action: They recompute the response over top Basement to top Latrobe only, excluding the carbonate-dominated Seaspray Group, to separate carbonate-module effects (Table 6, Figure 12).
steps.quote: response of each scenario to separate any different effects from the carbonate module.

steps.action: They extract depositional rates for the 102-68 Ma and 67-0 Ma phases and fit response equations with coefficients and t-values (Table 7, Figure 14).
steps.quote: Depositional rates can be extracted from the results for different phases

steps.action: They compare scenarios 4 and 10, which share high erodibility and low m but differ in fit, to show that interactions can counter a main effect (Table 8).
steps.quote: Table 8 compares scenario 4 which has a high erodibility but is a poor fit to the realistic model

steps.action: They keep the claim that the most significant controls are the stream-power-law variables (rainfall and m, erodibility and its interaction with m, critical slope and n), with others as moderate or secondary controls.
steps.quote: the most significant variables produced by the Badlands simulations can be related mostly to the amount of erosion via the detachment-limited stream power law

steps.action: Because initial topography matters only early, they set aside the concern that initial conditions control long-term outcomes in basin modelling.
steps.quote: the caution proposed by Perron and Fagherazzi (2012) is not a concern for basin modelling over long periods of time

steps.action: They explain the unexpected significance of sea level in the non-marine Early Cretaceous through Badlands drainage-area feedback, and compare the simulated inland seas and lakes with published fossil evidence.
steps.quote: which is confirmed by freshwater and marginal marine fossil occurrences probably including euryhaline biotas

steps.action: They keep the geological-history conclusions: mountains to the north, south and east were needed in the first syn-rift phase, and the modelled uplift fits empirical estimates of several kilometres.
steps.quote: This simple outcome had not been shown numerically before and has settled a debate that has continued for many decades.

tree.answer: Palaeo-landscape and basin-fill evolution of the Gippsland Basin, 137-0 Ma, under many interacting controls
No; the past landscape is known only from seismic, well and gravity traces built into a 3D model
Estimate the relative importance of the controlling variables through time
Candidate controlling variables screened by design; no stated rival hypotheses
Not formulated as distinct predictions; significance estimated by ANOVA
Set in the simulator by a 22-run fractional factorial design
Partly: compaction on/off, alternative response intervals, provenance and fossil consistency
Stream-power-law variables are the dominant controls; kept

end.claim: Across 22 designed Badlands scenarios fitted against the realistic 3D model, the most significant controls are those governing sediment supply via the stream power law (non-marine erodibility, rainfall, exponent m, slope and critical slope), with maximum % marine deposition also important. Sea level and subsidence matter only when fast enough to outpace supply, and controls change from rift to post-rift phases.

decisive_move.sentence: The ANOVA and response-equation fit in GSAT of the 22 designed scenarios' difference-map responses is what yields the significance ranking of the variables.

gates.evidence: No hypothesis directed data acquisition: field data were existing open-file seismic and well data, and the simulations screen candidate variables rather than test a stated hypothesis (p. 218-219). The claim could partly fail, since scenarios could have misfit the realistic model and variables could have been non-significant in ANOVA (p. 230-232); but the stream-power-law claim is not tested against an alternative law, which is declared out of scope (p. 218). The uncertainty framework and the 22-run ED were fixed before the final runs (p. 227), but variable ranges were adjusted after preliminary tornado charts (p. 230) and variables were screened iteratively (p. 227, 240).

imports.item: Design of experiments, fractional factorial designs (Montgomery 2017)
Morris (1991) factorial screening for deterministic computer experiments
ANOVA, multivariate response equations and tornado charts
GSAT scenario analysis tool for probabilistic reserve analysis (Collinson et al. 2008), run as an R wrapper

novelty_claims.quote: This simple outcome had not been shown numerically before and has settled a debate that has continued for many decades.

limits: Code from the published PDF only; the Supporting Information (GSAT explanation, variable details) and the companion thesis papers (Yang 2022) were not supplied, so method details there are not coded. The paper does not report how many preliminary sensitivity runs and range adjustments preceded the final ED (p. 221-230). The order of iteration is inferred: range adjustment (p. 230) logically preceded the final 22 runs but is reported after them. Inference: the realistic Petrel model both supplies the input isopachs and serves as the reference for fit, so the comparison is partly circular, although the authors state the forward simulations were not tied by the input maps (p. 229). No held-out data or second basin is used; the authors say other basins may need similar analysis (p. 236). With 22 runs and many terms, p-values are reported without a correction for multiple tests. Sub-claims at other statuses: (a) mountains to the north, south and east were needed in the Early Cretaceous (best_explanation, p. 222, 240); (b) the stream power law is 'satisfactory for modelling erosion in basins over deep time' (status none: no alternative erosion law was tested, p. 236); (c) the median land elevation is about a quarter of the missing-section thickness (regularity_in_range, inspection of scenarios only, p. 225); (d) different histories can produce similar present landscapes (best_explanation, p. 240). Composition none_fits: this is a designed computer-experiment sensitivity study conditioned on a reconstructed basin model. It is neither a trace series of independent observations nor strong inference among rivals, and it is not exploration-first, since the question precedes the runs.

disagreements.target: Field-based landscape evolution studies deriving basin-specific best-fit equations (e.g. Stock & Montgomery 1999; Murphy et al. 2016)
disagreements.support: The authors argue that region-specific fits are not transferable and confuse the identification of dominant variables; no new evidence is offered beyond the argument.
disagreements.quote: In these cases, the results are not generally applicable because each proposed model equation fits well with the specific dataset

disagreements.target: One-at-a-time sensitivity analyses of landscape models
disagreements.support: The authors argue such analyses cannot capture interactions, and later show significant interaction terms (Tables 5-7) and the scenario 4 versus 10 contrast (Table 8).
disagreements.quote: Running sensitivity analyses for supposed key variables in a large number of simulations is time consuming and can be misleading

disagreements.target: Bayesian and inversion calibration of landscape models (Barnhart et al. 2018, 2020; Fernandes et al. 2019; Stanley et al. 2020)
disagreements.support: The authors argue these approaches need many runs and prior guesses that can force outcomes; no direct comparison is made.
disagreements.quote: this invariably requires a number of simplifications or prior guesses for the input parameters that can force outcomes

disagreements.target: Perron & Fagherazzi (2012) on the legacy of initial conditions in landscapes
disagreements.support: In their simulations the initial topography's significance declines after the first syn-rift phase.
disagreements.quote: the caution proposed by Perron and Fagherazzi (2012) is not a concern for basin modelling over long periods of time

disagreements.target: Seismic stratigraphic studies on the role of marine accommodation space (see also Mutto & Steel 2000)
disagreements.support: ANOVA shows maximum % marine deposition is only a moderate control.
disagreements.quote: is a moderate control and is less important than perhaps envisaged in seismic stratigraphic studies

disagreements.target: Simple sediment-supply versus accommodation concepts in basin analysis
disagreements.support: The response equations show significant interactions, and very different simulated histories end with similar landscapes.
disagreements.quote: Simple concepts of sediment supply and accommodation space produced by sea level changes and subsidence or uplift are not sufficient.

disagreements.target: Long-running debate on the Early Cretaceous sediment sources of the Gippsland rift
disagreements.support: Sensitivity runs show only highlands to the north, south and east balance the sediment budget, consistent with provenance data; the opposing positions are not named.
disagreements.quote: This simple outcome had not been shown numerically before and has settled a debate that has continued for many decades.
